newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians hope troops will help restore peace.
newsitem.headline: Albanians hope troops will help restore peace.

text.p: Weary Albanians welcomed the arrival of foreign troops on Tuesday after months of unchecked violence, saying they hoped the force would bring peace to the chaotic Balkan state.
"I am delighted the force is here," said Artan Hoxha, a 36-year-old lawyer, as he sipped a coffee in a Tirana cafe.
"They will help bring back peace. If the force does a good job of protecting aid deliveries and if it wins people's confidence, then maybe it should be allowed to take weapons from people," he added.
At a busy market in central Tirana, a former solder named Thoma said he was glad the troops had finally reached Albania, but added the force should not try to disarm the nation.

"It's good the soldiers are here," said the 45-year-old man who declined to provide his last name as he sorted shirts on a stand in the open air market. "People will realise now we haven't been forgotten. The soldiers will make it easier for our police to chase criminals.
"I doubt any Albanians will attack the foreign soldiers, but if they do, the soldiers should respond. Only the Albanian police should take weapons away from our people," he said.
Italian officials have said the Italian-led eight-nation force would have the right to self-defence, but they were not authorised to disarm Albanians.
Soldiers on the mission called "Operation Alba" would not stand by and watch if they see violence against individuals -- as was the case at times with U.N. peacekeepers in Bosnia.
"The soldiers won't see Albanians fight each other," said Bejto Malo, a 36-year-old journalist. "The soldiers will help distribute aid by day, the Albanians kill each other by night."
Albania's leading newspapers hailed the landing and the biggest independent daily Koha Jone said in a page one headline: "Operation Alba arrives with hope for Albanians."
The Gazeta Shqiptare daily said: "Soldiers of peace arrive."
Flutra Xhani, a 45-year-old economist, said as she shopped at the market: "I would prefer it if the foreign soldiers disarmed people. I don't like to hear shooting."

Albania, Europe's poorest country, is awash with guns since people looted armouries, abandoned by police and soldiers, during an uprising that followed the failure of fraudulent savings schemes earlier this year.
Almost 300 people have been killed during two months of near-anarchy. Rebel-held committees control much of the south, blaming President Sali Berisha, a northerner, for the loss of their money.
Nearly 1,200 Italian, French and Spanish soldiers landed in Albania on Tuesday and fanned out across the country at the start of their mission to deliver emergency food and medicines.
Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino welcomed them, saying they would help restore peace and order.
"The government of Albania extends its best thanks in the name of the Albanian people for the readiness they have demonstrated in helping us at this delicate time," Fino said.
Etleva Beqolli, an unemployed 20-year-old, said she feared the aid would not reach many needy Albanians.
"How will the foreigners know which families to help? There are so many who need it," she said.
Relief agencies are targeting aid to hospitals, orphanages and homes for the elderly and handicapped, as well as destitute families. Officials say one in 10 people need aid.
Gani Saliasi, a 50-year-old technician, said the multinational force would set a good example to the Albanian police and encourage them to restore law and order.

"Only the restoration of order will convince people to give up their arms," he said, standing by the offices of a pyramid investment scheme where he and dozens of others waited, hoping to be reimbursed for their investments.
Saliasi had deposited a sum equivalent to $8,000 -- about eight years' pay for the average Albanian -- in a pyramid scheme.
Saliasi said he kept a Kalashnikov rifle at home because he was not convinced the police could protect him.
"I am ready to hand my weapon in as soon as I am sure that order has been restored in this country," he said.
